author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell reflects on what fatherhood has actually taught him, that you can't truly be a father to anyone else until you're a father to yourself first, a sense that who you are is already enough. He pushes further into a bigger cultural observation, that most of us are fed a message our entire lives that we're insufficient until we acquire the right body, possessions, approval, or affiliations. His sharpest point lands on success itself, questioning whether people we call driven are really just being dragged by insecurity and shame, chasing achievement to outrun a feeling of not being enough. A genuinely reflective moment on fatherhood, self worth, and what actually motivates ambition.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell gets refreshingly honest about a moment of pure ego, visiting Brixton Prison for a reading event alongside Jason Statham and Benedict Cumberbatch, and admitting his first thought was worrying about his place in the pecking order rather than the actual prisoners. He takes it further with an even more absurd confession about once being invited to international hostage negotiations and immediately wondering what he should wear.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell gets told he’s about to become a “kangaroo mom,” and things unravel almost immediately.

After meeting an agile wallaby and a baby red kangaroo, Russell goes from calling the pouch a “little sack of magic” to panicking about his feet, parasites and the animal getting anywhere near him. Before long, he’s standing on a chair while everyone else seems perfectly relaxed.

What starts as an adorable animal encounter quickly turns into Russell trying to get the kangaroo as far away from him as possible.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Dr. Stella Immanuel tells Russell why her views on childhood vaccination changed so dramatically, saying she would no longer take or administer another shot without stronger evidence convincing her of its benefits.

The conversation moves into her concerns about rising autism diagnoses, ADHD, SIDS and chronic illness, as well as her belief that Amish communities offer an important comparison because of differences in lifestyle and healthcare practices. Russell listens as Dr. Immanuel explains why these observations led her to question assumptions she once accepted as a trained pediatrician.
